What is stored, and how to remove it
Search for a setting, or open Privacy centre below.
Adds social tracking on top of the chosen level
Standard blocks the categories Firefox tracks by default. Strict blocks more, and can break sign-in flows and sites that fingerprint for fraud checks.
Cryptomining and fingerprinting scripts, cross-site tracking cookies, query-parameter stripping in private windows, and tracking-parameter removal from links.
Standard reduces the information a site can read back. Strict also disables APIs a site uses to tell one browser from another, which some sites treat as a sign of automation.
Canvas, WebGL, fonts, audio and screen metrics are reduced together by the level above. GeckoView exposes no way to relax them one at a time, so no switch is offered for them.
Blocking third-party cookies stops advertising and analytics scripts reading what you do elsewhere. Blocking all cookies breaks sign-ins, and is not the default.
Tries HTTPS before falling back to HTTP. There is no separate \"HTTPS-first\" mode: the engine exposes one setting with these three levels.
A certificate that does not validate stops the load with a local error page. There is no way to click through it, and no setting to add an exception.
Your DNS provider can see the names you look up. Encrypted DNS hides them from the local network, not from the provider you choose.
When on, a page classified as malware, phishing or deceptive is blocked and counted as a threat rather than a tracker.
Website to browser prompt to Android permission to your decision

A site asking for the camera, the microphone, your location or notifications gets a prompt in the browser first, and an Android permission only if you say yes. Denying either is remembered for that site.
Camera, microphone, location at the Android level
What is removed when the browser closes
Only what the engine actually reports is counted. GeckoView exposes no figure for third-party requests blocked, HTTPS upgrades or per-site tracking, so none is shown.
Cache, cookies, site data, history, bookmarks, passwords and downloads are separate. Nothing is bundled with anything else.
The engine can clear all of a category or none of it; it cannot clear \"the last week\" of cookies or cache. History is stored by the browser, so the History screen can delete by date.
The shortcut that searches when you type words
Suggestions send what you have typed to the search provider. Turning every list off is the private choice.

Tabs, their back-forward history and their scroll position, plus recently closed tabs. Private tabs are deliberately left out.

Windows a site opens on its own. Links you tap still open.
The default answer for a site that starts sound or video without you tapping play. You can still change it per site.
Installers, scripts, double extensions and unencrypted transfers

Saved logins are offered through an encrypted vault that lives on this device. Nothing is synchronized, and nothing is sent anywhere. Filling a login into a form depends on the engine\'s field-focus events.
A passkey is created and used by the engine.
WebAuthn runs inside GeckoView and exposes no embedder hook, so there is nothing for the shell to switch on or off. Passkeys work where the engine supports them; this build has no setting for them.
Audio continues when you switch tabs or apps
Float a playing video over other apps
Bluetooth routing needs no permission: audio reaches a paired headset through the platform audio stack, which is why the browser declares no Bluetooth permission at all.
Applies a floor to text the engine renders. Sites that set their own sizes keep them above the floor. Android\'s own display size scaling still applies on top.
This GeckoView build ships no zoom API, so per-site zoom is not offered. Pinch-to-zoom on a page still works.
What the browser can measure honestly. The engine exposes no per-category size for cookies, cache or site storage, so none is shown rather than estimated.
Remote debugging is available in debuggable builds only. An ordinary release neither shows the switch nor enables the socket, so a setting carried over from a debug install cannot open it.
GeckoView exposes no proxy API, so proxying is left to the system or a VPN app. There are no experimental features in this build, so there is no list to gate: nothing is offered that is not finished.
Most breakage is a permission the site asked for and you denied.
Open Site permissions to see what this site was allowed, and change it. If the site needs a desktop layout, Request desktop site is the other common fix.
Resets preferences only. Bookmarks, history, downloads and saved passwords are left alone; use Clear browsing data to remove those.
Every setting returns to its shipped default. Bookmarks, history, downloads and saved passwords are not touched.
What this app is built from
GeckoView and its dependencies are licensed by Mozilla and the Apache and Kotlin projects. No analytics, advertising or crash-reporting SDK is present in this build.

Nothing leaves this device unless you ask it to.

Search suggestions are sent to the search provider you chose, and only while suggestions are on. The DNS provider you choose can see the names you look up. Extension updates are fetched from the add-on source you added them from.

There is no account, no sync, no analytics and no crash upload. Crash reports are written to this device only, and you can read them in Diagnostics.
Every line is read from the running browser. Nothing here is estimated, and nothing is sent anywhere.
Trackers and threats blocked so far

Some banks refuse anything that is not a common desktop browser. A compatibility switch: it adds a fingerprint.

These are the decisions this site already has. Tapping one flips it between allowed and blocked; the change takes effect the next time the site asks.
This site has not asked for anything, so there is nothing to relax. If it is not working, a desktop layout is the usual reason.
A browser built for people who would rather not be tracked. It runs on the real Gecko engine, the same one Firefox uses, so websites get the engine they expect.
Unofficial. LibreWolf is a separate project from the LibreWolf desktop browser, and this app is not affiliated with either.
You do not have to configure anything to be private. These are the defaults, and every one of them is yours to change later.

No accounts, no telemetry, nothing sold to anyone

LibreWolf asks for notification access for two things: to show download progress and to let a website show its own notifications when you allow it. It is asked once. If you say no, you will not be asked again by a site, and you can turn it on later in Settings.
